title: The ledger of hours
hook: we guard our money closely and hand out our time to anyone who asks

segments.voice: Yesterday: Seneca, who said life isn't short, only wasted. Long enough, if used. Today, the ledger.

A stranger asks for twenty dollars, no reason. The answer is no, probably without a thought. A stranger asks for twenty minutes: a survey, a sales call, a meeting that could have been an email, a video that autoplays into the next. Those get handed over all day long. Seneca noticed the same strange double standard, in yesterday's essay. We guard our money. We give our time to anyone who asks.
screen: `TWENTY DOLLARS? NO.` → `TWENTY MINUTES? SURE.` → `WE GUARD THE WRONG THING.`

segments.voice: In the essay's third chapter, people won't let anyone take an inch of their land, Seneca says. One boundary dispute and they're off to court, with stones and weapons. But they let others walk right into their lives, and even invite them in. Nobody hands out their money; everybody hands out their life. Tight-fisted with property, wildly generous with the one thing it would be right to be stingy with: time. Then a clever move. He asks a man who's reached old age to go through the ledger. Take your years and subtract. How much went to a creditor, to a patron you had to flatter, to quarrels at home, to errands around the city? Subtract all that, and you have fewer years than you counted. In the first of his letters to his friend Lucilius, it's one line, in Richard Gummere's translation: "Nothing, Lucilius, is ours, except time." A house can be taken, money lost. Time is the one thing put in your hands alone, and the one thing nobody ever returns. He doesn't say never give it away. Friendship, service, love: those take hours, and they're worth it. His point is the ledger. Know where it goes. Choose where it goes. Guard at least one hour the way you'd guard your wallet.
screen: `NOT AN INCH OF LAND.` · `WILDLY GENEROUS WITH TIME.` · `GO THROUGH THE LEDGER.` · `NOTHING IS OURS, EXCEPT TIME.` · then, large: `GUARD ONE HOUR.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle. Picture tomorrow as a ledger, morning to evening, and notice which hours are already spoken for. Then find one hour you'd truly choose to guard, for a walk, a friend, a book or rest, and picture yourself saying no, kindly, to what would take it.
Seneca. His reminder that we guard our money and give our time away, when time is all that's truly ours.
Your line: time is the only property. It's the one thing put in your hands alone. Day thirty-one, done.

howItsDone: People who follow Seneca's advice often keep an account of their time, as he told Lucilius he did, and deliberately protect some hours for what they value most.

chat.says: Why did Seneca say time is the only thing that's truly ours?
options: A house can be taken and money lost, but time is in your hands alone.
Because time, unlike money, can be saved up now and spent later.
Because friendship and service only waste the hours we're given.
chat.meaning: Nothing is ours except time, he wrote to Lucilius. He didn't say never give it away: know where it goes, and choose where it goes.
